items.prompt: What is 'curiosity-driven learning,' as this unit defines it?
choices: Learning pursued because it's genuinely interesting or solves a problem currently in front of you
Learning that only happens during scheduled work hours
Learning that always takes less than an hour
Learning assigned by a manager as part of a formal plan
items.explanation: Curiosity-driven learning is defined by its trigger — a real question or problem — not by when it happens or who assigned it.
items.reference:
Curiosity-driven learning
triggered by a real question or problem
tends to stick, because there's a real use attached

Why: What triggers the learning — not how it looks from outside — is what predicts whether it sticks.

items.prompt: Why does curiosity-driven learning tend to be retained better than anxiety-driven learning, according to this unit?
choices: Because it's tied to a real question or use, rather than to the mere existence of something new
Because it always involves more total hours of study
Because it's always done in a classroom setting
Because it only happens for topics that are already easy
items.explanation: Retention tracks the reason the learning started — a real question gives the material somewhere to attach, unlike a launch-triggered urgency that fades once the feeling passes.
items.reference:
Curiosity-driven learning
triggered by a real question or problem
tends to stick, because there's a real use attached

Why: What triggers the learning — not how it looks from outside — is what predicts whether it sticks.

items.prompt: What is 'anxiety-driven learning,' as this unit defines it?
choices: Learning pursued mainly to avoid the feeling of falling behind, driven by the existence of the new thing rather than a real question
Learning that involves feeling nervous before an exam
Any learning done outside of business hours
Learning that is always factually incorrect
items.explanation: Anxiety-driven learning is defined by its trigger — the new thing existing at all — not by any particular emotion during study or the time of day it happens.
items.reference:
Anxiety-driven learning
triggered by the new thing's existence, not a real question
shallow, often forgotten once the urgency passes

Why: It's the version most likely to burn hours without building anything durable.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, the folder of half-finished courses is best explained by which pattern?

A lack of any technical ability
A deliberate, well-planned curriculum
Courses assigned by a manager and later cancelled
items.explanation: The pattern — urgent at the start, abandoned once something newer shows up — is the signature of anxiety-driven learning: the trigger is the launch, not a real question.
items.reference:
Anxiety-driven learning
triggered by the new thing's existence, not a real question
shallow, often forgotten once the urgency passes

Why: It's the version most likely to burn hours without building anything durable.

Churn rate
~15 new significant things/year (this unit's estimate)
mostly fixed, not under your control

items.reference:
Sustainable absorption capacity
bounded by hours available, not just willpower
the side of the ratio you can actually manage

Why: Increasing this indefinitely isn't the fix — hours in a week are fixed regardless of urgency.

items.explanation: There's no achievable 'caught up' state because the churn rate doesn't stop or wait — treating it as a finish line guarantees permanent, low-grade failure at an unreachable target.
items.reference:
Keeping up isn't a finish line

the useful question: did I learn what moves my goals forward

Why: Retargeting the goal is what makes growth measurable and achievable again.

anxiety: triggered by a launch, evaporates once urgency fades

items.prompt: What does L2's 'relevance' filter question ask?
choices: Whether the new thing connects to a problem in your current work or a goal you actually hold
Whether the new thing is free to learn
Whether the new thing has more than 1,000 stars on a code-hosting site
Whether a coworker has already learned it
items.explanation: Relevance is about connection to real, current work or goals — not popularity metrics, cost, or what a coworker happens to have done.
items.reference:
Three filter questions
relevance — connects to current work or a real goal?
durability — likely to matter in two years?
genuine interest — a real question pulling you, not just hype?

Why: A 'no' to all three is the clearest signal the pull is anxiety, not a real reason to learn.

Three filter questions
relevance — connects to current work or a real goal?
durability — likely to matter in two years?
genuine interest — a real question pulling you, not just hype?
